checks.query: How should an ecommerce brand create a tech pack and approve factory samples before bulk production?

cards.title: Run the Sample Progression: Strike-Off to Pre-Production to Production
cards.summary: Advance through three sample stages and hold a factory sample as the gold standard reference so bulk orders can be checked against it.
cards.use_when: You are selecting between final candidate factories or preparing to green-light bulk production.
steps: Order samples from every potential supplier you are considering — this tests communication and reliability as much as quality. Watch who follows instructions, sends updates unprompted, and matches your tech pack precisely.
Start with a strike-off or small test sample to approve materials and prints.
Move to a pre-production sample that should match your tech pack perfectly. Treat this as the gold standard you will compare bulk against.
For apparel, confirm grading here: get multiple pre-production samples to verify sizes scale correctly (S, M, L proportions).
Keep one approved sample in-house and one at the factory for reference.
After choosing the final supplier, order a production sample built right before mass production. If it does not match the pre-production standard, do not proceed.
Protect your IP as you scale: keep original tech packs, artwork and source files on your side, sign a manufacturing agreement at volume, and register trademarks.
caveats: The source presents the production sample mismatch as a hard stop; it does not discuss scenarios where minor deviation might be acceptable.
Grading guidance is specific to apparel sizing.
cards.source_name: The Ultimate Guide To Product Sourcing In 2026.docx

cards.title: Approve a new factory sample before committing to a store launch
cards.summary: Never pitch factory-sourced product to a buyer without first obtaining and inspecting a physical sample from that factory.
cards.use_when: Selecting a new supplier or product variation before placing a bulk purchase order for an ecommerce store.
steps: Collect samples from each candidate factory for any new product or new supplier.
Inspect the sample for the quality attributes your client or store depends on before making any pricing or listing commitments.
Use approved sample quality and a complete cost quote to decide whether to commit to production and customer-facing promises.
Keep the sample as the reference for the bulk run, so your quality check has a fixed benchmark.
Combine sampling with your external vetting: the source builds client trust on saving time and reducing risk, not just lowering cost.
caveats: A good sample does not guarantee a good bulk run — production quality can drift, so build in pre-shipment checks.
Sampling adds cost and lead time, which matters most for fast-moving ecommerce launches.
cards.source_name: How He Makes Millions Sourcing Products From China.docx

cards.title: Build a Tech Pack Before Contacting Any Factory
cards.summary: A tech pack is the product blueprint that stops factories from guessing on materials, colors, measurements and packaging, which is the root cause of inconsistent shipments.
cards.use_when: You are preparing to source a new physical product or reorder an existing one and need to lock specifications before requesting factory quotes.
steps: Draft a single document that defines exactly how the product must be built, from materials through packaging. Factories optimize for throughput, not your brand, so anything undefined gets replaced with whatever is easiest for them.

Include: detailed product drawings or photos from every angle; exact materials and finishes including GSM, trims and hardware; measurements for every size or variant; colorways with Pantone codes; label, packaging and care instructions; and a clear product name, version and date.
If you are not a designer, hire one. The source notes experienced product designers on Upwork can build a tech pack for around $200, and calls it worth the cost.
Keep specs current using Figma, Canva or Notion templates so every reorder references the same version.
Treat every reorder as a gamble until a tech pack exists: without it you may get lucky once but cannot build consistency across orders.
caveats: Tech pack cost and freelancer availability are the source's example, not a guaranteed price. Verify current marketplace rates.

The source's cautionary example is a blanket brand that received three different shades of gray and different weights in one SKU because no spec sheet was ever sent — results are illustrative, not a benchmark.
cards.source_name: The Ultimate Guide To Product Sourcing In 2026.docx

cards.title: Write Exact Measurements in Spec Sheets, Never Vague Terms
cards.summary: Replace subjective descriptors like 'centered' in tech packs with precise dimensions so factories cannot make their own interpretation decisions.
cards.use_when: A seller is writing a tech pack, spec sheet, or decoration placement instructions for a factory before a production run.
steps: Do not write 'centered' — the source notes factories won't match your mental model of centered, and orientation ambiguity (is it centered this way or that way?) is a common failure.
Specify exact offsets: e.g. '4 inches from the top, 4 inches from the bottom, 2 inches from the side, 2 inches from the side.'
Apply the same rule to every dimension, color reference, and imprint location in the tech pack.
Aim for the rule of making all decisions yourself and letting the factory make none; any decision you leave open is one they'll guess wrong.
Build a step-by-step checklist of production checks (the source describes an ~80-step sourcing process) and require the team to tick each box before shipping.
caveats: Exact spec sheets reduce errors but don't eliminate risk — the source still pairs them with reference samples and pre-production sampling.
The 80-step figure is the source's internal process, not a required or validated standard.
cards.source_name: How He Makes Millions Sourcing Products From China.docx

cards.title: Keep Your Product Factory-Ready Before You Message Suppliers
cards.summary: Most sourcing problems start with the product definition, not the factory: unclear specs cause suppliers to guess, cut corners and produce inconsistent stock.
cards.use_when: You are defining a new product or fixing recurring inconsistency across reorders before you start supplier outreach.
steps: Get crystal clear on every specification before contacting any supplier. The source's own early experience: a blanket shipment arrived with three different shades of gray and different weights in the same SKU because no spec sheet had been sent.
Reframe the failure as your own: factories do not see your brand the way you do; they optimize for throughput and efficiency, so undefined details default to whatever is easiest for them.
Build the tech pack described in these cards as the single source of truth for materials, measurements, colorways, trims and packaging.
Treat inconsistency across reorders as a specification problem until proven otherwise.
Once specs are defined, supplier sourcing becomes easier because suppliers cannot take shortcuts and you are no longer guessing.
caveats: The three-shades-of-gray incident is the source's personal example, used to illustrate the cost of unclear specs, not a typical defect rate.
The source insists a tech pack is not optional for serious product quality — an opinion, not an industry-wide mandate.
cards.source_name: The Ultimate Guide To Product Sourcing In 2026.docx

checks.query: How do we compare supplier quotes using bill of materials, landed cost and volume price breaks?

cards.title: Ask for Volume Price Breaks on Every BOM Line
cards.summary: Negotiate component-level price breaks tied to unit volumes, understanding that factory economics rest on machine and labor utilization.
cards.use_when: Setting up volume tiers with a factory, planning a purchase order schedule, or forecasting COGS at higher volumes.
steps: For each BOM line (cotton, labor, zippers, polishing/QC, etc.), ask: at what volume does this price drop?
Frame it around the supplier's utilization — how much of their dedicated line is used, where is idle machine or fixed-labor capacity you can fill?
Reconcile invoices with the supplier line-by-line (the source has production leads sit with suppliers to do this), so credits for hitting thresholds are actually applied.
Track price breaks on sub-components too, since suppliers pass through their own sub-vendor economies of scale (e.g. a big zipper maker gives the factory a discount that should flow to you).

Consider internalizing procurement of key components (buying gold/diamonds/chips directly and supplying your assembler) to capture the sub-vendor margin, but only once you can manage the inventory price risk.
caveats: The source frames these as credits applied after you hit overage volumes, not blanket discounts — build the mechanism into the agreement. Internalizing components also exposes you to commodity price swings.
cards.source_name: He Went From $3M In Debt To $13M In Cash Using This Playbook.docx

cards.title: Build a Bill of Materials Before Anything Else
cards.summary: A bill of materials breaks unit cost into every component and sub-vendor so COGS becomes a controllable, negotiable line instead of a mystery number.
cards.use_when: Setting up or renegotiating product sourcing for any physical-goods store, and before you start sourcing a new SKU or assume your landed cost is fixed.
steps: List every component of the finished unit (e.g. a gold solitaire ring = diamond, gold, labor, factory overhead, factory margin).
For each component, capture: component cost, sub-supplier/source, lead time, country of origin, and payment terms.
Get the sub-vendor layer too — your factory may not make its own inputs (lab-grown diamonds, gold, zippers, chipsets).

Split out labor and factory overhead as separate lines; these are the hardest to ask about but the ones that reveal where the money is. Verify sourcing claims (e.g. test that 'organic cotton' is actually organic).
Track component prices that move intraday or monthly (gold, diamonds, chipsets) so a supplier's markup stays visible and you can reprice when markets move.
Review the BOM with your supplier at least yearly and request price-break thresholds per line item.
Use the BOM as the first audit when acquiring or taking over a store: ~99 of 100 founders in the source's M&A experience did not have one.
caveats: The source says a BOM is worth building once you spend roughly $1M/year on COGS (~$100k/month to supplier), and some businesses benefit as low as ~$2.5M annual revenue; it is a judgment call below that.
cards.source_name: He Went From $3M In Debt To $13M In Cash Using This Playbook.docx

cards.title: Use Volume Quotes to Reset Your Unit Cost Baseline
cards.summary: Post RFQs at multiple volume tiers to find how far per-unit cost falls, then weigh the discount against cash flow and defect risk.
cards.use_when: Product selection or replenishment: you are reordering a proven SKU and want to know whether moving from small Aliexpress-style batches to a bulk Alibaba order is worth the capital lock-up.
steps: Confirm the SKU already sells at a healthy margin before scaling. The source's jewellery example sold at $7.80 cost / $25.99 retail from weekly 500-unit batches.

Post several Request For Quotation (RFQ) listings on Alibaba for the same product rather than accepting the first quote, because the same item appeared anywhere from $10 down to $4.00 depending on order size.

Ask each supplier to quote explicitly at your target volume (the source cites ~10K units landing near $2.00 per unit versus $7.80 in small batches) plus one tier below and one above, so you see the slope of the discount.

Compare the discount against the cash required and the storage risk of holding that inventory; a deep unit-cost cut is not automatically the better decision if it ties up working capital you need elsewhere.
Treat all figures as example quotes from one jewellery case, not benchmarks — your category, material and current market will differ.
caveats: Volume discounts are the source author's experience with jewellery, not a general pricing guarantee.

A commenter with sourcing/manufacturing background notes that unused volume or freight-consolidation discounts can be more valuable leveraged in other ways (e.g. cash-flow structures) than taken as a straight price cut.
cards.source_name: What I learnt from sourcing e-commerce products from China.docx

cards.title: Bill of Materials as the Foundation of Supply Chain Profit
cards.summary: A bill of material (BOM) is the foundational layer for any physical-goods business and the starting point for supply chain optimization and cash extraction.
cards.use_when: Setting up or auditing sourcing and COGS for a physical product store, or planning a cost-reduction or margin-improvement initiative across SKUs.
steps: Build a complete bill of materials for every sellable SKU: all components, packaging, inserts, and variable costs (shipping, duties, fees) that make up true landed cost.
Treat the BOM as the base of the profit pyramid — everything downstream (management accounts, free cash flow, distributions) depends on it being accurate.
For stores already doing millions in revenue, reconcile the BOM against actual supplier invoices and freight costs to find gaps and margin leaks.
Use the BOM to standardize margin accounting across all SKUs, and revisit it whenever a cost input (freight, packaging, supplier pricing) moves.
caveats: Speech-to-text garbled 'BOM' as 'bum' — the actual concept is bill of material.
The claim that BOM is 'by far' the most foundational input is the source's opinion, framed as advice to operators of physical goods.
cards.source_name: He Went From $3M In Debt To $13M In Cash Using This Playbook.docx

cards.title: Compare supplier credit with other working-capital options
cards.summary: The goal across BOM, price breaks and terms is a supplier relationship where they finance your inventory and dividends.
cards.use_when: Designing your overall sourcing/finance strategy and deciding what to prioritize as you scale purchasing.
steps: Stack the levers in order: BOM for cost visibility, then component price breaks, then long payment terms, then consignment.
Compare actual dated payments, fees, required security and downside obligations across supplier credit and alternatives; the source's lender cost examples are not current quotes.
Express financing charges in currency and over the financed period; an annual rate on a balance is not automatically the same percentage of COGS or revenue.
Keep the supplier relationship collaborative and share your vision so they become an eager partner rather than a lender of last resort.
Choose terms that preserve cash under slower sell-through, defects and delays rather than assuming every saving should fund more advertising.
caveats: This is Roman Khan's stated approach; results are his own and reflect a specific business mix and scale, not a guarantee. Long terms and consignment still require a supplier willing to extend them.
cards.source_name: He Went From $3M In Debt To $13M In Cash Using This Playbook.docx

checks.query: How should we inspect product quality before shipment and qualify a backup supplier?

cards.title: Book a Pre-Shipment QC Inspection Before the Container Leaves
cards.summary: A third-party QC inspection before shipment catches defects while the factory can still fix them; once goods are on the water, problems cannot be corrected.
cards.use_when: A production run is finishing at the factory and you are about to approve final payment and shipment.
steps: Before the container leaves the factory, book a third-party quality control inspection.
The source cites a rough cost of about $200 per inspection, framing it as insurance against far larger losses from damaged or inconsistent stock.
Have the QC agent test random units, check measurements, verify packaging and labeling, and check carton weight.
Require the agent to photograph everything and flag even small inconsistencies that could become larger issues later.
If problems are found, the factory fixes them before the shipment departs.
Approve or reject the shipment based on the QC report and release final payment only once everything passes.
caveats: The $200 cost and a '$20,000 saved' figure are the source's illustrative numbers, not validated benchmarks; get current quotes from inspection providers.
The source frames the inspection as effectively mandatory before shipment.

cards.title: Maintain a vetted supplier shortlist by product category
cards.summary: The scarce part of sourcing isn't finding a factory but finding the best one, so build a curated factory library you can plug clients into.
cards.use_when: A seller or agency is deciding how to build a defensible sourcing advantage or differentiate from Alibaba-based competitors.
steps: Recognize that mediocre product is easy: anyone can filter Alibaba and get a decent item.
Treat the hard, valuable work as finding the best-of-the-best factory for each product category (best t-shirts, best hats, etc.).
Record qualified factories, capabilities, approved samples and observed performance by product category and region.
Use the shortlist to reduce repeated sourcing work and production risk when adding a SKU; do not assume prior approval covers a materially different product.
For your own ecommerce store, apply the same logic: your factory relationships and vetted quality are a moat, not the sourcing itself.
caveats: Building a curated factory library takes years per the source, so this is a long-term asset, not a launch shortcut.
Even curated factories need ongoing re-vetting and backup suppliers.
cards.source_name: How He Makes Millions Sourcing Products From China.docx

cards.title: Test New Suppliers With Small Batches Before Switching
cards.summary: Run a cheaper supplier through a small test order while keeping your incumbent, and only migrate after verifying quality.
cards.use_when: Supplier negotiation or cost reduction: you've found a vendor quoting materially less and are tempted to move your whole order.
steps: Keep your current supplier active. The source explicitly warns against ditching a supplier too early.
Place a limited test order with the cheaper supplier — the author's example was 500 units against a cost that was ~20% lower than the incumbent.
Inspect the test batch before committing volume. In the source's case most of the 500 units were defective, which would have been catastrophic at full order size.
Maintain multiple qualified vendors so you always have a fallback if one fails inspection or raises prices.
Only migrate your supply chain once the new supplier has proven defect rates comparable to your incumbent; until then, treat the cheaper quote as a hypothesis, not a saving.
caveats: This is a risk-management heuristic from one bad experience, not a guarantee that cheap suppliers fail.
A test batch adds cost and lead time; factor that into the decision.

- If problems are found, the factory fixes them before the shipment departs.
- Approve or reject the shipment based on the QC report and release final payment only once everything passes.
Caveat: The $200 cost and a '$20,000 saved' figure are the source's illustrative numbers, not validated benchmarks; get current quotes from inspection providers.
Caveat: The source frames the inspection as effectively mandatory before shipment.

[101cb1f841d99d0a183bfd2a] Approve a new factory sample before committing to a store launch
Use when: Selecting a new supplier or product variation before placing a bulk purchase order for an ecommerce store.
- Collect samples from each candidate factory for any new product or new supplier.
- Inspect the sample for the quality attributes your client or store depends on before making any pricing or listing commitments.
- Use approved sample quality and a complete cost quote to decide whether to commit to production and customer-facing promises.
- Keep the sample as the reference for the bulk run, so your quality check has a fixed benchmark.
- Combine sampling with your external vetting: the source builds client trust on saving time and reducing risk, not just lowering cost.
Caveat: A good sample does not guarantee a good bulk run — production quality can drift, so build in pre-shipment checks.
Caveat: Sampling adds cost and lead time, which matters most for fast-moving ecommerce launches.

[f759ab73c73c1b1edfff8de5] Maintain a vetted supplier shortlist by product category
Use when: A seller or agency is deciding how to build a defensible sourcing advantage or differentiate from Alibaba-based competitors.
- Recognize that mediocre product is easy: anyone can filter Alibaba and get a decent item.
- Treat the hard, valuable work as finding the best-of-the-best factory for each product category (best t-shirts, best hats, etc.).
- Record qualified factories, capabilities, approved samples and observed performance by product category and region.
- Use the shortlist to reduce repeated sourcing work and production risk when adding a SKU; do not assume prior approval covers a materially different product.
- For your own ecommerce store, apply the same logic: your factory relationships and vetted quality are a moat, not the sourcing itself.
Caveat: Building a curated factory library takes years per the source, so this is a long-term asset, not a launch shortcut.
Caveat: Even curated factories need ongoing re-vetting and backup suppliers.

[28b7e903d4ef11f4373ceac8] Test New Suppliers With Small Batches Before Switching
Use when: Supplier negotiation or cost reduction: you've found a vendor quoting materially less and are tempted to move your whole order.
- Keep your current supplier active. The source explicitly warns against ditching a supplier too early.
- Place a limited test order with the cheaper supplier — the author's example was 500 units against a cost that was ~20% lower than the incumbent.
- Inspect the test batch before committing volume. In the source's case most of the 500 units were defective, which would have been catastrophic at full order size.
- Maintain multiple qualified vendors so you always have a fallback if one fails inspection or raises prices.
- Only migrate your supply chain once the new supplier has proven defect rates comparable to your incumbent; until then, treat the cheaper quote as a hypothesis, not a saving.
Caveat: This is a risk-management heuristic from one bad experience, not a guarantee that cheap suppliers fail.
Caveat: A test batch adds cost and lead time; factor that into the decision.

[aa2d7527a54d637d435c7d75] Keep Your Product Factory-Ready Before You Message Suppliers
Use when: You are defining a new product or fixing recurring inconsistency across reorders before you start supplier outreach.
- Get crystal clear on every specification before contacting any supplier. The source's own early experience: a blanket shipment arrived with three different shades of gray and different weights in the same SKU because no spec sheet had been sent.
- Reframe the failure as your own: factories do not see your brand the way you do; they optimize for throughput and efficiency, so undefined details default to whatever is easiest for them.
- Build the tech pack described in these cards as the single source of truth for materials, measurements, colorways, trims and packaging.
- Treat inconsistency across reorders as a specification problem until proven otherwise.
- Once specs are defined, supplier sourcing becomes easier because suppliers cannot take shortcuts and you are no longer guessing.
Caveat: The three-shades-of-gray incident is the source's personal example, used to illustrate the cost of unclear specs, not a typical defect rate.
Caveat: The source insists a tech pack is not optional for serious product quality — an opinion, not an industry-wide mandate.

checks.query: How do we calculate a reorder point using sales velocity, replenishment lead time and safety stock?

cards.title: Calculate Reorder Point with Velocity, Lead Time and Safety Stock
cards.summary: Reorder Point = (Daily Sales Velocity x Total Lead Time) + Safety Stock, so you reorder before running dry rather than chasing demand.
cards.use_when: You are setting reorder triggers and planning replenishment shipments for any SKU.
steps: Measure daily sales velocity: how fast the product actually sells, measured over time. Use Shopify order history to spot velocity, slow movers and seasonal spikes, and review weekly.
Measure replenishment lead time from releasing a reorder until usable stock is received, including production, freight, customs and receiving; payment date alone may not start the operational clock.
Set a safety stock buffer to cover sales spikes or freight delays so you keep selling.
Compute: Reorder Point = (Daily Sales Velocity x Total Lead Time in days) + Safety Stock.

Example: 50 units/day x 60 days + 500 safety units = 3,500 units. Compare against inventory position: usable on-hand plus confirmed inbound minus committed or backordered demand, avoiding double-counting allocations.
Feed weekly performance and stock-level reviews into the reorder plan, and communicate them to suppliers before problems appear.
caveats: The example numbers are illustrative inputs, not benchmarks; your velocity, lead time and safety stock must come from your own data.
The source attributes a major stockout and lost sales to having no forecasting system in place — treat the formula as a discipline, not a one-time calculation.
cards.source_name: The Ultimate Guide To Product Sourcing In 2026.docx

cards.title: Build a Weekly Forecasting Rhythm Even as a Solo Operator
cards.summary: Forecasting is not an afterthought: assign someone or a weekly ritual to review velocity, lead times and stock so demand spikes don't leave you sold out for months.
cards.use_when: You need a repeatable operating cadence to keep sourced products in stock and profitable, whether you are solo or have a small team.
steps: Create a simple system that forces a performance and stock-level review every single week.
Include daily sales velocity, total lead time and safety stock in the same sheet you use for the reorder point calculation.
Communicate stock and forecast positions to suppliers proactively, before problems appear.
If possible, designate one person focused purely on operations and planning rather than splitting the role.
Start planning the next shipment when the current one lands, since production plus transit can consume 50-70 days in total.

Treat the failure mode as a planning failure, not bad luck: the source describes a demand spike to $200,000/day sales followed by a sellout, months-long lead times and nearly two months unable to fulfill orders.
The source believes a dedicated operations/planning focus could have made that business 30-40% bigger — its own retrospective estimate, not a universal figure.
caveats: The 30-40% upside figure is the source's retrospective opinion about its own business, not a benchmark for yours.
The source states you do not need a full team to start — discipline and a weekly cadence suffice initially.
cards.source_name: The Ultimate Guide To Product Sourcing In 2026.docx

cards.title: Choose Air vs Sea Freight with a Hybrid Strategy
cards.summary: Blend air freight for speed and sea freight for margin, choosing based on product size, weight and urgency rather than always taking the cheapest rate.
cards.use_when: You are planning how to move a finished production run from factory to warehouse.
steps: Air is fast and expensive — suited to small, urgent batches or very small products.
Sea freight is slower but dramatically cheaper and keeps margins healthy at scale.
Most successful brands the source describes use a hybrid: air a small batch to start selling quickly, then follow with sea shipments to restock at lower cost.
Adjust to product characteristics: small items suit a mix; large or heavy items almost always favor sea.

Plan lead times backwards. Sea can take 30-40 days door-to-door, air 7-10 days, and production itself adds roughly 20-30 days. If you wait until you are nearly out of stock to reorder, you are already late.
Start planning the next shipment the moment your current one lands.

Use a freight forwarder for container booking, customs and delivery coordination. Do not simply chase the cheapest forwarder — the source warns the cheapest may leave goods sitting at port for weeks to fill a container.
caveats: Transit and production day ranges are the source's typical estimates, not guarantees; confirm current lead times with your forwarder.
The source notes freight forwarders quote based on route, weight and deadlines.
cards.source_name: The Ultimate Guide To Product Sourcing In 2026.docx

cards.title: Use Volume Quotes to Reset Your Unit Cost Baseline
cards.summary: Post RFQs at multiple volume tiers to find how far per-unit cost falls, then weigh the discount against cash flow and defect risk.
cards.use_when: Product selection or replenishment: you are reordering a proven SKU and want to know whether moving from small Aliexpress-style batches to a bulk Alibaba order is worth the capital lock-up.
steps: Confirm the SKU already sells at a healthy margin before scaling. The source's jewellery example sold at $7.80 cost / $25.99 retail from weekly 500-unit batches.

Post several Request For Quotation (RFQ) listings on Alibaba for the same product rather than accepting the first quote, because the same item appeared anywhere from $10 down to $4.00 depending on order size.

Ask each supplier to quote explicitly at your target volume (the source cites ~10K units landing near $2.00 per unit versus $7.80 in small batches) plus one tier below and one above, so you see the slope of the discount.

Compare the discount against the cash required and the storage risk of holding that inventory; a deep unit-cost cut is not automatically the better decision if it ties up working capital you need elsewhere.
Treat all figures as example quotes from one jewellery case, not benchmarks — your category, material and current market will differ.
caveats: Volume discounts are the source author's experience with jewellery, not a general pricing guarantee.

A commenter with sourcing/manufacturing background notes that unused volume or freight-consolidation discounts can be more valuable leveraged in other ways (e.g. cash-flow structures) than taken as a straight price cut.
cards.source_name: What I learnt from sourcing e-commerce products from China.docx

cards.title: Automate procurement from weekly to daily purchase orders
cards.summary: At thousands of SKUs, custom software can move PO placement from weekly to daily with consistent logic, improving replenishment responsiveness.
cards.use_when: Managing replenishment and purchase orders for a high-SKU ecommerce catalog.
steps: Recognize the operational constraint: with thousands of SKUs, weekly PO cycles are hard to run well manually; the presenter built custom software to place POs daily.
Encode replenishment logic in the system so daily POs follow rules rather than manual judgment each time.
Treat this as a build-once system (the presenter's team built it for themselves) rather than a per-cycle cost.
Look ahead to agentic supply chain: the presenter's goal is an AI agent that talks to supplier agents and places orders automatically based on real sell-through volume.
caveats: Requires development resources; the presenter built custom software for his own business.
The agent-to-agent vision is a stated future goal, not a described working system yet.
